'''Manley Lanier "Sonny" Carter Jr.''', [[Doctor of Medicine|M.D.]] (August 15, 1947 – April 5, 1991), ([[Captain (United States O-6)|Capt]], [[United States Navy|USN]]), was an American [[physician]], professional [[soccer]] player, [[United States Navy|naval officer]], [[United States naval aviator|aviator]], and [[NASA]] [[astronaut]] who flew on [[STS-33]].

==Early life and education==
Carter was born on August 15, 1947, to parents Manley L. Carter and Elizabeth C. Carter in [[Macon, Georgia]], but considered [[Warner Robins, Georgia]], to be his hometown.<ref>{{cite web |title=Sonny Carter's biography |url=https://www.nasa.gov/sites/default/files/atoms/files/carter_manley_0.pdf |date=April 1991 |publisher=NASA |access-date=November 17, 2020}}</ref> He graduated from [[Central High School (Macon, Georgia)|Lanier High School]] in Macon in 1965, and during his high school years was actively involved in the Macon-based Troop 19 of the [[Boy Scouts of America]], where he also served a term as [[Senior Patrol Leader]], the highest leadership position for a young man in that BSA troop, and earned its highest rank of [[Eagle Scout (Boy Scouts of America)|Eagle Scout]].<ref>[http://www.scouting.org/About/FactSheets/scouting_space.aspx Sonny Carter at scouting.org] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303213130/http://www.scouting.org/about/factsheets/scouting_space.aspx |date=March 3, 2016 }}</ref>

Carter received a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in [[chemistry]] from [[Emory University]] in [[Atlanta]] in 1969, and a [[Doctor of Medicine]] degree from there in 1973. During his time at Emory, Carter was a brother in the [[Alpha Tau Omega]] fraternity. After completing [[Emory University School of Medicine]] in 1973, Carter completed [[Internship (medicine)#United States|internship]] in [[internal medicine]] at [[Grady Memorial Hospital]] in Atlanta.{{citation needed|date=July 2026}}

==Athletic career==
Carter played collegiate [[soccer]] and ran [[track and field|track]] while an undergraduate at [[Emory University]]. During his senior season, he was [[Captain (association football)|captain]] and [[most valuable player]] of the soccer team. In addition to his intercollegiate athletic career, Carter was an intramural [[Scholastic wrestling|wrestling]] champion. He played professional soccer while he attended medical school. In 1970, he signed with the [[Atlanta Chiefs]] of the [[North American Soccer League (1968–1984)|North American Soccer League]] (NASL), for which he played three seasons.<ref>[http://www.nasljerseys.com/Players/C/Carter.Manley.htm Manley Carter career stats], North American Soccer League, NASLJerseys.com</ref>

==Navy service==
{{unreferenced section|date=July 2026}}
In 1974, Carter entered the [[U.S. Navy]] and completed [[flight surgeon]] school in [[Pensacola, Florida]]. After serving tours as a flight surgeon with the [[1st Marine Aircraft Wing|1st]] and [[3rd Marine Aircraft Wing]]s, he returned to flight training at [[Beeville, Texas]], and was designated a [[Naval Aviator]] on April 28, 1978. He was assigned the senior medical officer of the [[aircraft carrier]] {{USS|Forrestal|CV-59|6}}, and in March 1979 completed F-4 training at [[VMFAT-101]] in [[Marine Corps Air Station Yuma]], [[Arizona]]. He was subsequently reassigned as a [[fighter pilot]], flying [[F-4 Phantom]]s with Marine Fighter Attack Squadron 333 ([[VMFA-333]]) at [[MCAS Beaufort]], [[South Carolina]]. In 1981, he completed a nine-month [[Mediterranean]] cruise aboard USS ''Forrestal'' with [[VMFA-115]]. In September 1982, he attended [[United States Navy Strike Fighter Tactics Instructor program|U.S. Navy Fighter Weapons School]] ([[TOPGUN]]) and then served as the [[2nd Marine Aircraft Wing]] standardization officer and F-4 combat readiness evaluator at [[MCAS Cherry Point]], [[North Carolina]]. He then attended the [[U.S. Naval Test Pilot School]], graduating in June 1984.

Carter logged 3,000 flying hours and 160 carrier landings.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Manley L. "Sonny" Carter, Jr. |url=https://www.amfcse.org/manley-l-sonny-carter-jr |access-date=2026-09-28 |website=AMF CSE |language=en-US}}</ref>

==NASA career==
Selected by NASA in May 1984, Carter became an astronaut in June 1985, qualified for assignment as a [[mission specialist]] on future [[Space Shuttle]] flight crews.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-05-23 |title=40 Years Ago: NASA Selects its 10th Group of Astronauts - NASA |url=https://www.nasa.gov/history/40-years-ago-nasa-selects-its-10th-group-of-astronauts/ |access-date=2026-09-28 |language=en-US}}</ref>

===Space Shuttle program===
{{Main|STS-33}}
[[File:STS-33 crew.jpg|thumb|right|Sonny Carter (standing row, left) with his STS-33 crewmates]]
Carter was assigned as [[Extra-vehicular activity]] (EVA) Representative for the Mission Development Branch of the Astronaut Office when selected to the crew of [[STS-33]]. The STS-33 crew launched from [[Kennedy Space Center]], [[Florida]], at night on November 22, 1989, aboard the Space Shuttle [[Space Shuttle Discovery|''Discovery'']]. The mission carried [[United States Department of Defense|Department of Defense]] payloads and other secondary payloads. After 79 [[orbit]]s of the Earth, this five-day mission concluded on November 27, 1989, with a hard surface landing on Runway 04 at [[Edwards Air Force Base]], [[California]]. Carter logged 120 hours in space.{{citation needed|date=July 2026}}

At the time of his death in April 1991, Carter was assigned as mission specialist 3 on the crew of [[STS-42]] ''Discovery'', the first International Microgravity Laboratory (IML-1). His place was taken by [[David C. Hilmers|Dave Hilmers]].{{citation needed|date=July 2026}}

==Death==
{{Main|Atlantic Southeast Airlines Flight 2311}}
Carter died in the April 5, 1991, crash of [[Atlantic Southeast Airlines Flight 2311]] in [[Brunswick, Georgia]]. He was aboard the commercial airplane traveling for NASA.<ref>[https://www.ntsb.gov/ntsb/brief.asp?ev_id=20001212X16773&key=1 National Transportation Safety Board Brief]</ref> His wife Dana and two daughters, Olivia Elizabeth (born May 27, 1974) and Meredith Corvette (born December 3, 1976), were not on the flight.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.spaceacts.com/starship/seh/vanhoft.htm |title=Sonny Carter's family |access-date=October 9, 2015 |archive-date=December 23, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181223030057/http://www.spaceacts.com/starship/seh/vanhoft.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref> Among the others who also died in the plane crash was [[John Tower]], a former [[United States Senate|senator]] from [[Texas]].<ref>{{Cite news |title=John Tower, Daughter, Astronaut, 20 Others Killed in Plane Crash |url=https://apnews.com/f9552fdcecb32f0bfebacac866a700d9 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230101010358/https://apnews.com/f9552fdcecb32f0bfebacac866a700d9 |archive-date=January 1, 2023 |access-date=May 24, 2026 |work=AP NEWS |language=en|last=Sanchez|first=Joan|date=April 5, 1991}}</ref>

Carter's death occurred on the same day as the launch of the [[Space Shuttle Atlantis|Space Shuttle ''Atlantis'']] on mission [[STS-37]].{{citation needed|date=July 2026}}

==Organizations==
Carter was a member of the Society of U.S. Naval Flight Surgeons, Sigma Delta Psi, [[Alpha Omega Alpha]], [[Alpha Tau Omega]], the [[United States Marine Corps|Marine Corps]] Aviation Association, the [[Tailhook Association]], and the [[Society of Experimental Test Pilots]].{{citation needed|date=July 2026}}

==Special honors==
*[[Air Medal]]
*[[Meritorious Service Medal (United States)|Meritorious Service Medal]]
*[[Navy Achievement Medal]]
*[[Meritorious Unit Citation]]
*[[United States Marine Corps|Marine Corps]] Aviation Association Special Category Award (1982)
*NASA Meritorious Service Medal (1988)
*[[NASA Space Flight Medal]] (1989)

Carter was the guest of honor at the 215th [[United States Marine Corps birthday ball|Marine Corps Birthday Ball]].{{citation needed|date=July 2026}}

==Legacy==
[[File:Space Mirror Memorial Sonny Carter.JPG|thumb|right|Space Mirror Memorial Sonny Carter]]
Having died in the line of duty for NASA, Carter's name was added to the [[Space Mirror Memorial]] at [[Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex]] in [[Merritt Island, Florida]]. His name was the first added after the memorial's original construction.{{citation needed|date=July 2026}}

After his death, his name was given to the [[Sonny Carter Training Facility]] [[Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory]], NASA's underwater astronaut training facility, for which he had developed training techniques.{{citation needed|date=July 2026}}

In 1989, Emory University inducted him in its Athletic Hall of Fame.<ref>[http://www.emory.edu/EMORY_MAGAZINE/winter97/alumnimsg.html#anchor1385195 Honoring the true student athlete], ''Emory Magazine'', Emory University, Winter 1997.</ref> The university holds '''The Sonny Carter Invitational''' each year in his honor. A plaque also honors his memory in the library of the [[Alpha Tau Omega]] [[college fraternity|fraternity]] house at Emory, in which he was a Brother.{{citation needed|date=July 2026}}

[[File:20-02-034-aviation.jpg|thumb|right|Plaque of Carter at the [[Georgia Aviation Hall of Fame]]]]

In 1992 he was inducted into the [[Georgia Aviation Hall of Fame]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Manley L. "Sonny" Carter Jr. |url=http://www.gaaviationhalloffame.com/Hall-of-Fame.48.0.html?avid=24 |access-date=October 9, 2018 |website=Georgia Aviation Hall of Fame |archive-date=June 2, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170602001727/http://www.gaaviationhalloffame.com/Hall-of-Fame.48.0.html?avid=24 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

Sonny Carter Elementary School in Macon, Georgia, which opened in 1993, was named for Carter. The school motto is: "To Challenge the Edge of the Universe."{{citation needed|date=July 2026}}

The Society of United States Naval Flight Surgeons (SUSNFS) bestows an annual "Sonny Carter Memorial Award" to the nominee with the most significant contribution to the health, safety and welfare of the operational forces by promoting communication and teamwork amongst the aeromedical community.<ref>{{cite web |title=Sonny Carter Memorial Award SUSNFS |url=http://www.susnfs.org/SUSNFS/awards.htm |access-date=May 6, 2019 |archive-date=June 27, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220627201026/http://www.susnfs.org/SUSNFS/awards.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref>
